items.reason: Source locates the wrinkles: "resembling in the pleated watery wrinkles bordering it, the polished metallic-like marks". Candidate "in its pleated watery wrinkles" drops "bordering it" (the wrinkles edge the sleek; they are not on it).
items.new: The shrewd thinking behind these movements was sufficiently proved at daybreak by the sight of a long sleek on the sea directly and lengthwise ahead, smooth as oil, and resembling, in the pleated watery wrinkles bordering it, the polished metallic marks of some swift tidal rip at the mouth of a deep, rapid stream.

items.reason: Source "With oars apeak" is the specific whaleboat posture (oars peaked, blades raised clear of the water, as in ch. 48 and elsewhere), not merely "at rest".
items.new: With oars peaked, blades raised clear of the water, and paddles down, the sheets of their sails adrift, the three boats now silently floated, awaiting Moby Dick's reappearance.

items.reason: Source "sailed hard upon the breeze" means close-hauled. "sailed close into the breeze" reads as heading into the wind's eye; the idiom is "close to the wind".
items.new: Because of the way she had been steering, the wind had been somewhat on the Pequod's quarter; so now, pointed in the reverse direction, the braced ship sailed close to the wind as she churned up again the cream of her own white wake.

items.reason: Source "the line ran through the grooves" is plural; candidate "through the groove" changes the detail.
items.new: The harpoon was darted; the stricken whale flew forward; with igniting speed the line ran through the grooves — ran foul. Ahab stooped to clear it; he did clear it; but the flying turn caught him round the neck, and, as voicelessly as Turkish mutes bowstring their victim, he was shot out of the boat before the crew knew he was gone. The next instant, the heavy eye-splice at the rope's final end flew out of the stark-empty tub, knocked down an oarsman, and, striking the sea, disappeared in its depths.
